statement: A flag has 3 stripes, one above another. Each stripe is red, white or blue, and two stripes that touch must be different colours. How many different flags are possible?

choices.misconception: I gave the two lower stripes 2 choices each and multiplied, but forgot the 3 choices for the top stripe.
I used each colour exactly once, but the top and bottom stripes may match because they do not touch.
I gave every stripe only 2 choices, even the top one, which can be any of the 3 colours.
I gave the top and middle stripes 3 choices each and forgot about the bottom stripe.

hints: Choose the colours one stripe at a time, from the top down.
Use the multiplication principle stripe by stripe. The top stripe can be any colour; each stripe below only has to be different from the one just above it.
Top: 3 choices. Middle: any colour except the top one, so 2 choices. Bottom: any colour except the middle one, so 2 choices. Total 3 x 2 x 2 = 12.

solutions.reliable: The top stripe can be red, white or blue: 3 choices. Whatever it is, the middle stripe can be either of the other 2 colours. The bottom stripe must differ only from the middle one, so it also has 2 choices, and it may match the top. Total 3 x 2 x 2 = 12 flags. The transferable idea: when each choice limits only the next one, count the choices step by step and multiply.
solutions.elegant: Flags using three different colours: 3 x 2 x 1 = 6. Flags whose top and bottom match: 3 colours for those two stripes and 2 for the middle, so 6. Total 6 + 6 = 12.

whyOnTest: A rule about touching stripes changes the count at each step, which tests whether students apply the multiplication principle carefully.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
